title: 人工智能与数字化转型时代的佛教伦理
abstract: 数字化转型加速了人工智能对社会生活的影响，传统伦理体系遭遇前所未有的挑战，而佛教拥有的智慧及严格的戒律要求，因果的法则，将成为人工智能的伦理治理提供有效的参考。本文先厘清人工智能发展现状及问题，然后系统讨论数字化场景中佛教修行及传播所面临的新问题，由此引出研究目标及核心问题：AI伦理可借鉴佛教“缘起性空”思想，促进人机良性互动，避免技术滥用。但佛教伦理在数字化转型中也面临信仰形式异化、传统遭解构、伦理落地难等问题。本文提出融合佛教智慧构建多元共治的AI伦理体系、推动佛教自身数字化良性转型、搭建人机共生的伦理体系等路径，让技术发展与人文伦理彼此协调、互为促进，最终实现“科技为体，佛法为魂”的良性互动。

title: 短视频中生成式人工智能的法律风险与规制
abstract: 随着短视频平台兴起与生成式人工智能技术的发展，生成式人工智能技术与短视频内容的生产与传播深度融合，在激发创作者创作动力的同时，也催生著作权侵权、人格权侵害以及数据安全泄露等多种法律风险。这类风险的传播路径有别于一般网络侵权，现行以避风港原则为核心的平台责任框架已经难以应对。本文通过对三类典型风险进行系统性梳理，进而从规范体系、侵权责任主体以及因果关系认定三个角度分析我国短视频中生成式人工智能的规制困境。在此基础之上，提出制度方案以实现权益保护与技术促进的动态平衡。

title: The Dogma of the Legal Unprotectability of Style
abstract: This research critically challenges the traditional dogma that styles are not eligible for legal protection against the backdrop of the GenAI revolution. AI tools enable anyone to generate new images, musical works and texts in the style of their favourite artists within seconds and at little or no cost. This raises the question of the extent to which styles may qualify for legal protection and whether such protection is desirable in the first place. Remarkably, legal scholarship that firmly maintains that styles are not eligible for legal protection has failed to clearly define what should be understood by ‘style’. Accordingly, this study first examines the meaning of ‘style’. In the absence of a legal definition, an interdisciplinary approach was adopted. The meaning of ‘style’ was explored across the disciplines from which legal scholarship has drawn the concept: linguistics, music and the visual arts. For the purposes of this study, ‘style’ is understood exclusively as a set of formal characteristics that recur consistently within a particular group of creations. Where these creations can be attributed to a single creator, the term ‘personal style’ is used. Where, by contrast, the creations originate from different creators but are related on some other basis, the term ‘general style’ is used. Examples include the style of a particular period, school, region or culture. Through a comparative legal study of the Netherlands, the United States and the United Kingdom, this research examines the protection of personal and general styles under copyright law, design law and unfair competition law.

title: A Comparative Analysis of Clustering Algorithms in Targeted Preventive Care
abstract: In the modern healthcare, the importance of preventive care has came out as an effective approach in order to lighten the load of hospitals while also ensuring prolonged life span for patients. The current study on Clustering algorithms in targeted preventive care, highlights one such major issue in clustering algorithms that help uncover hidden patterns from a dataset to generate more precise preventative ac- tions in medical care. The core of this study involves a detailed comparative study of different clustering algorithms: K-Means, DBSCAN and Hierarchical Clustering. The methodology used in this study in- volves using various health datasets containing such features as age, body mass index, diabetes, asthma, arthritis, life style factors and geographical location, etc. The main evaluation factors to consider in regard to the algorithms include Silhouette scores metric, Scalability, Robustness and Interpretability. The results of this analysis, K-Means proves to be very efficient when dealing with huge, well-defined datasets. For this reason, it is suitable for population screening. However, when considering identification of outliers in patients having rare or unusual health problems, DBSCAN shows much better results. On the other hand, Hierarchical clustering gives much better insight into nesting various health risks. This report also focus on preprocessing, including scaling of data and handling incomplete values. Another interesting point of the analysis is that besides simple classification of health data, it may help predict chronic diseases, discovering some symptoms that would remain unnoticed during manual examination.

title: SmartPost AI: An AI-Assisted Framework for Intelligent Professional Content Creation and Automated LinkedIn Management
abstract: The rapid development of Large Language Models (LLMs) has had a significant impact on the area of AI-assisted content generation, providing capabilities to generate coherent context-aware text for different purposes. However, current solutions of AI writing assistants are limited in terms of addressing all aspects of professional content management, which include contextual information retrieval, organization, scheduling, persistent cloud storage, and automated publishing. Therefore, users are required to use several separate solutions, making their workflow less efficient and more labour-intensive. In this paper, we introduce SmartPost AI - an end-to-end framework for AI-assisted professional content creation and LinkedIn management. The framework utilizes the combination of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), LLMs, cloud-based data management, and LinkedIn API-based publishing, all integrated in one multi-layered architecture. The proposed framework enables users to provide either text prompts or web-based content, retrieve relevant contextual information, generate LinkedIn posts in professional format, convert Markdown output into Unicode-based formatting, and manage content centrally via secure storage, scheduling, and publishing capabilities. The framework is deployed as a cloud-based full-stack web application using Next.js, FastAPI, Supabase , and LinkedIn APIs. Deployment and experiment of the framework prove that the AI-based content generation, workflow orchestration, cloud storage, and auto-publishing features have been implemented successfully in one coherent framework. The suggested framework simplifies the process of content creation and makes it more automated, creating the basis for the intelligent AI-assisted content management and publishing system.

title: Artificial intelligence and machine learning in Islamic banking: insights using lexicon and machine learning-based models
abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) within the Islamic banking sector, focusing on sentiment analysis of these technologies across annual reports from 71 full-fledged Islamic banks in 16 countries between 2015 and 2023. Design/methodology/approach The authors used five sentiment analysis models, TextBlob, valence aware dictionary and sentiment reasoner, AFINN, long short-term memory (LSTM) and bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT), to assess sentiment polarity and word frequency of AI and ML terms using Python. Sentiment distributions and trends were analysed across time, country and individual banks using visualisations from R Studio. Findings The results indicate a predominantly positive sentiment towards AI and ML in Islamic banking, with advanced models like LSTM and BERT capturing nuanced sentiment more accurately than traditional models. Regional differences emerged, with countries like Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE demonstrating notably higher positive sentiment levels. The findings reveal significant sentiment variations among models, countries and banks, emphasising AI and ML’s perceived value in enhancing efficiency, compliance and customer experience. Research limitations/implications The study’s reliance on annual reports may limit sentiment scope, suggesting future research could expand to other data sources for a comprehensive view. Practical implications The findings offer valuable insights for Islamic banks, regulators and stakeholders to inform responsible AI adoption and its application in enhancing service quality and regulatory compliance. Originality/value This research fills a notable gap by examining AI and ML sentiment in Islamic finance, providing new insights into stakeholder perspectives on these technologies’ role and impact.

title: Optimizing Ship Heading Control Using an Improved Dung Beetle Algorithm for PID Control
abstract: Due to the time-lag characteristics of ship motion, traditional PID-based heading control algorithms have difficulty achieving the desired control accuracy. The study introduces a control method derived from the enhanced Dung Beetle Optimization algorithm. Initially, the Nomoto model serves as the vessel dynamics simulation. Subsequently, the algorithm’s objective function is honed through a blend of Elite opposition-based learning, the golden sine strategy, and an acrobatic “Somersaulting” technique for foraging, thereby bolstering its global exploration prowess, sidestepping pitfalls of local optima, and expediting the convergence trajectory. Finally, the optimized parameters are input into the control system to simulate ship directional motion. The findings indicate that employing the refined Dung Beetle Optimization technique to tweak the PID control variables yields a substantial enhancement in the ship’s steering capabilities. This approach effectively minimizes overshooting during course corrections and allows the control system to steadfastly keep the vessel on track, consistently at the designated heading.

title: Code and data for central-spin revival and recovery
abstract: Numerical data and analysis code for the companion article Revival tolerance and recovery after coupling drift in a central-spin bath. The archive includes 40 static-profile recovery points, 36 changed-profile points, independent circuit checks, and the inputs and scripts for four figures. It comes with reproduction instructions, a dependency list, and SHA-256 checksums. The archive retains the attribution and Apache 2.0 license for the upstream QuAIR circuit material. No general license has been specified for the other files.

title: MICRO1 VALE A PENA? CONHEÇA AS VAGAS REMOTAS PARA TRABALHAR COM INTELIGÊNCIA ARTIFICIAL
abstract: O mercado de inteligência artificial está crescendo rapidamente e, juntamente com ele, estamos criando oportunidades para profissionais que desejam trabalhar remotamente em projetos de treinamento, avaliação e aprimoramento de modelos de IA. Mas, com tantas plataformas disponíveis na internet, uma pergunta é bastante comum: qual plataforma de treinamento de IA é confiável? Uma das empresas que estamos acompanhando de perto neste segmento é a Micro1 , uma plataforma que conecta profissionais de diferentes áreas e oportunidades relacionadas ao desenvolvimento e treinamento em inteligência artificial. Se você deseja saber mais sobre este mercado e encontrar oportunidades internacionais, visite a plataforma através deste link: https://omeulink.com/Micro1Ai Neste artigo, explicaremos como funciona o Micro1, quais atividades podemos realizar, como participar do processo seletivo e quais cuidados devemos tomar antes de nos candidatarmos. O QUE É MICRO1? A Micro1 é uma empresa que conecta profissionais especializados a projetos relacionados ao treinamento e aprimoramento de modelos de inteligência artificial. A proposta é reunir pessoas com experiência em diferentes áreas para ajudar os sistemas de IA a compreender informações, resolver problemas, produzir melhores respostas e executar tarefas com maior precisão. Entre os segmentos em que podemos encontrar oportunidades na plataforma estão: Programação e desenvolvimento de software; Engenharia de software; Inteligência artificial e aprendizagem de máquina; Finanças e contabilidade; Áreas da medicina e da saúde; Certo; Educação e pesquisa; Marketing e comunicação; Linguística e línguas; Análise de dados. Isso significa que as oportunidades não se destinam exclusivamente a programadores. Profissionais com experiência em outras áreas também podem encontrar projetos compatíveis com seus conhecimentos. Para consultar as oportunidades disponíveis, acesse: https://omeulink.com/Micro1Ai O MICRO1 É CONFIÁVEL? Essa é uma das principais dúvidas de quem encontra uma oportunidade de trabalho pela internet. A Micro1 apresenta as características de uma operação comercial real: possui um site oficial, um portal de oportunidades, um processo de avaliação de candidatos e informações públicas sobre o funcionamento de seus projetos. A empresa também explica que conecta especialistas a trabalhos relacionados ao desenvolvimento de sistemas de inteligência artificial. Seu processo inclui candidatura, entrevista ou avaliação de habilidades, certificação e possível encaminhamento para projetos. Entretanto, é importante entender a diferença entre uma plataforma legítima e uma garantia de obtenção de trabalho. Uma plataforma pode ser real e ainda assim não oferecer projetos imediatamente para todos os candidatos. A própria Micro1 informa que a aprovação da certificação não garante a contratação ou a participação imediata em um projeto. A seleção depende das habilidades demonstradas, dos requisitos de cada oportunidade e da disponibilidade de projetos. title: Paper IV — Immune-Gated Recursive Self-Improvement (IG-RSI), Acquired Cognitive Immunity & Tritemporal K-Time Consolidation
abstract: Conventional neural language models are epistemically static after deployment: either their parameters remain permanently frozen—forcing all adaptation into external retrieval databases (RAG / GraphDB) and brittle system prompts—or they undergo naive continual fine-tuning that rapidly degrades through model collapse, template overgeneralization, and self-reinforcing hallucination. In this paper, we formulate a biological and systems-engineering alternative: Immune-Gated Recursive Self-Improvement (IG-RSI). We propose that genuine neural evolution requires pairing recursive weight consolidation with an Acquired Cognitive Immune System—an adaptive internal defense architecture that recognizes logical contradictions, premise reversals, surface-similarity traps, and false self-verifications before experiences migrate from episodic memory into slow neural weights. Drawing on empirical multi-round evolution experiments on the 32-layer hybrid linear-attention model MiniMinX (Qwen3.5-32L Gated-DeltaNet + Full-Attention + Sovereign Titan Crown), we report three core contributions: 1. Three-Tier Neural Cognitive Immunity: We formalize an immunological hierarchy across (Tier 1) Innate Epistemic Barriers (SleepConsolidationGate C1-C6, separating memory type from reliability), (Tier 2) Adaptive In-Trajectory Negative Selection (surface-invariant moral and causal discrimination across minimal pairs), and (Tier 3) Selective Cortical Internalization (freezing the lower linguistic spine L00-L15 at 0.0 bit drift while consolidating verified habits into the upper corridor L16-L31 and LowRankSleepMoEBank). 2. Isolation of Four Empirical Cognitive Pathogens: We document and resolve four failure modes discovered during recursive self-improvement: (I) Autoimmune Over-Triggering on Surface-Similar Twins (urgent countdown triggers vs. true life-safety stakes), (II) Induction-Head Suffix Copying during methodological repair, (III) Short-Template Attractor Collapse (L_SFT < 0.06), and (IV) Internal Metadata Tag Reification. 3. Executable Tritemporal K-Time Sleep Consolidation (Operationalizing 10.5281/zenodo.23198458): We integrate the six-state Tritemporal K-Time epistemic maturity clock (UNKNOWN -> WILD -> CANDIDATE -> GREYBOX -> MATURE -> REVOKED) directly into a PyTorch SleepConsolidationGate with authority-weighted slow synaptic plasticity (lambda_eff = lambda_slow * a_i). Verification confirms that unverified WILD claims (a_i = 0.0) and revoked claims produce 0.00000000 slow-weight corruption, while multi-turn verified MATURE propositions (a_i in [0.85, 1.00]) consolidate smoothly into slow weights.

title: Multimodal AI fusion for colorectal cancer survival prediction
abstract: This research poster presents a multimodal deep learning study for predicting overall survival in colorectal cancer. The study uses patient-matched whole-slide images (WSIs), structured clinical data, and survival outcomes from the MCO (1,375 patients) and TCGA (555 patients) cohorts, with a 59-month analysis horizon. The study compares WSI-only models, a tabular FT-Transformer, and a multimodal hypergraph that uses cross-attention to incorporate clinical features into the image representation. Models were assessed using the concordance index (C-index) through patient-level cross-validation within each cohort and external validation in both directions. The multimodal hypergraph outperformed all WSI-only models across the four validation settings. When pathology and staging variables were excluded, it also outperformed the tabular model in both external validations. The FT-Transformer with all variables achieved the highest mean C-index in every setting (0.715–0.766). Future work will investigate which tissue features provide complementary prognostic information and develop an agentic AI layer to support model selection, hyperparameter exploration, experiment tracking, and comparison of fusion strategies.

title: Anomaly Detection in Time Series with Enhanced Privacy Using Self-Supervised Contrastive Learning
abstract: Anomaly detection in time series is increasingly used for sensitive data, including medical and physiological data. However, these data carry a substantial risk of information leakage, making privacy preservation through anonymization essential. While anonymization reduces the risk of privacy breach, it can also remove informative features, creating a trade-off between privacy preservation and anomaly-detection performance. To address this challenge, we propose a robust framework that mitigates this trade-off and enables high-accuracy anomaly detection on anonymized data. Our approach centers on an anonymization function that transforms a time series by removing sensitive information, including contextual features and personally identifiable information, while retaining information that is beneficial for anomaly detection. We introduced a privacy model that guides the training of the anonymization function and optimizes the two components in an adversarial manner using contrastive loss in opposite directions. This design uses the anonymization function to eliminate sensitive information captured by the privacy model. We incorporate an anomaly detection loss function to ensure that the anonymization function preserves the essential information required for accurate anomaly detection. The effectiveness of the anonymization process and its impact on anomaly-detection performance were evaluated using multiple real-world and synthetic datasets. Results showed that our method reduced privacy-related information leakage by 42.65% while incurring only a 2.58% decrease in the F1 score for anomaly detection.

title: Self-Reported State Empathy in Response to Video Stimuli: Comparing the Measurement Characteristics of Cognitive and Affective Empathy
abstract: In this study, we propose an 8-item self-reported state empathy scale comprising four cognitive empathy (CE) and four affective empathy (AE) items to evaluate empathic responses to video stimuli on a per-trial basis and examine its measurement characteristics. For a scale to function as a state measurement, its scores must fluctuate according to the nature of the presented scene, rather than only with stable between-participant differences. Therefore, we had 10 participants repeatedly respond to 24 video stimuli and decomposed the variation in the resulting 240 trials into stimulus effects, participant effects, and residuals. We further conducted correlation analyses using the inclusion of other in the self (IOS) scale and emotion congruence as external criteria for AE and video accuracy rate as an external criterion for CE. In the AE subscale, 42.8% of the variance was attributed to stimulus effects and 8.9% to participant effects, and AE correlated positively with the IOS ( r =.772) and emotion congruence ( r =.308). evidence.abstract: In this study, we propose an 8-item self-reported state empathy scale comprising four cognitive empathy (CE) and four affective empathy (AE) items to evaluate empathic responses to video stimuli on a per-trial basis and examine its measurement characteristics. title: State-Vector Simulation of 36-Qubit Ekerå–Håstad Factoring Using FP8 Storage on Commodity NVIDIA GB10 Hardware
abstract: We report an exact state-vector simulation of the semiclassically folded Ekerå–Håstad (EH) short discrete-logarithm factoring circuit up to 36 logical qubits on commodity NVIDIA GB10 unified-memory hardware (121 GiB per node). Pairing IEEE FP8 (e4m3, 2 bytes per complex amplitude) state-vector storage with FP32/FP64 arithmetic kernels and host-side double-precision global scale tracking enables factoring 35-bit balanced RSA semiprimes on two GB10 nodes (242 GiB aggregate memory), while the same single-node architecture (np = 1, without MPI) scales to 35 logical qubits on a single GB10 or proportionally on discrete-VRAM commodity GPUs. Over 100 GbE RoCE (HPCX OpenMPI + UCX rc), the verified 36-qubit factorization of N = 24,966,154,091 = 157007 x 159013 completes its successful 53-round run in 1,339.8 s (2,688.7 s across two attempts). Both the folded EH circuit and 2-byte/amplitude rescaled storage follow established prior art (Ekerå; De Raedt et al., JUQCS-A); this technical note serves as an open-access defensive publication and engineering benchmark. Both English and Chinese PDF editions are included.

title: AetherMemory: Memory Lifecycle Integrity in Autonomous Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: AetherMemory is the twelfth candidate of the Aether family. It investigates whether persistent knowledge in autonomous multi-agent systems requires a distinct architectural dimension — a memory lifecycle — that cannot be reduced to storage (AetherGit), consistency (AetherMesh), policy (AetherPolicy), or audit (AetherAudit). Current status: Phase 0 (Architectural Hypothesis). Decision: (E) Undetermined (interim). No implementation exists. There is no src/, no tests/, no experiments/. The investigation is analytical. The repository contains: - The architectural hypothesis, with seven lifecycle stages (S1–S7) and five candidate responsibilities (M1–M5). - A responsibility boundary map against the eleven other Aether projects. - A falsification plan with four failure conditions (M-F1 to M-F4). - Partial execution of M-F1 (coverage analysis), M-F2 (composition analysis), and M-F3 (decentralization analysis). - A status declaration for M-F4 (not executable at Phase 0, requires Phase 5 and 6). - An independence decision: (E) Undetermined (interim). - An independent review by Jonathan Rabe (AI | ML Engineer, Angeles University Foundation), completed 2026-11-19. The reviewer confirmed the (E) Undetermined (interim) classification. - A research paper (v0.1.0), 9 figures, and full project documentation. Structural dependency: AetherMemory is structurally dependent on the resolution of AetherPolicy and AetherAudit, both paused at Phase 4. Any conclusion about AetherMemory is conditional on how those two investigations resolve. AetherMemory is a candidate, not a result.

title: A Continual Self-Supervised Learning Framework Using a Decoder and a Clustering-Based Data Selection Method
abstract: Continual learning aims to learn a sequence of tasks without forgetting the previously learned tasks. Promising methods for achieving continual learning include applying a replay buffer that stores previously learned samples in existing learning frameworks. Among these methods, lifelong unsupervised mixup (LUMP) interpolates the current task samples and samples from the replay buffer to prevent forgetting. LUMP randomly selects data for the replay buffer. This random selection is likely to have a negative effect on learning performance. In this study, we propose a clustering-based data selection method for the replay buffer. In addition, we introduce a denoising autoencoder to the self-supervised methods to improve the performance of the learning representations. We compare the clustering algorithms used in our framework and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework through computational experiments. Experimental results on CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet demonstrate that the proposed framework improves the average accuracy compared with LUMP while reducing forgetting. In particular, the CA+-based selection approach enhances the learning performance. The source code is available at https://github.com/Masuyama-lab/LUMP_SidAE_Clustering

title: Every Man Must Play a Part: After Hinton's Alarm
abstract: In two years the range of tasks AI systems can carry out has grown sharply, and they can now plan a task, execute it and evaluate the result in a cycle. The autonomous operation of machines has advanced in parallel, and AI now reaches physical space. What remains is adjustment and resources, and areas that do not yet pay are already objects of investment, because costs are certain to fall. The reach of AI ethics widens with this, from the behaviour of a system to the society it acts in. That something large is under way is widely sensed, and in November 2026 Geoffrey Hinton, a pioneer of the field, carried that sense as a warning to European Union leaders. The path from the widening to the conclusions drawn has not been set out. This commentary asks what follows from the widening and what does not. It examines the alarm's reasoning, which derives loss of control from a ranking of intelligence, a machine that wants and a competition that one party loses. It then turns from AI's position on a line of capability to how systems and their society are built: what it takes to understand an instruction, who answers for each component, and how harm arises where no machine wants anything and no builder intends it. The starting point is that a system as large as a society cannot be inferred from individual pieces of logic. On that view humankind is one system, with AI part of it.

title: Vertical Domain Large Language Models: Applications, Challenges, Future Prospects
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become a cornerstone of modern generative artificial intelligence, demonstrating remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks, including machine translation, question answering, and dialogue generation. However, most existing reviews primarily emphasize theoretical foundations and training methodologies, and offer limited insights into real-world application performance and domain-specific deployment patterns. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic literature review following PRISMA guidelines, synthesizing the application of LLMs across diverse vertical domains. The review examines system architectures, technical approaches, and performance benchmarks reported in the literature. In addition, it analyzes core challenges associated with LLM deployment, such as hallucinations, explainability, value alignment, and data quality, along with targeted solutions. Finally, it identifies emerging research opportunities and future directions, contributing to a more coherent, application-oriented understanding of LLM development and impact.

title: A Benchmark Hit Is Not an Exposure: What Published Vision-Language Geolocation Accuracy Says About Location Privacy, Why One Model Locates 61 Percent of One Photo Set to a Kilometre and Fewer Than 12 Percent of Another to a Hundred, and the Exposure Estimand a Privacy Claim Needs
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research Since 2024 a growing literature has argued that general-purpose vision-language models can work out where a photograph was taken well enough to make image geolocation an immediate privacy risk, and a second literature has begun building defences against it. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the direction of that claim survives the evidence but its usual support does not: the accuracies quoted for it are properties of particular photo sets, adversaries and distance thresholds, and none of them is the quantity a privacy claim is about. The same model places 61 percent of a curated, text-rich stock-photo set within one kilometre, about 23 percent of a public Flickr benchmark, and fewer than 12 percent of sampled street-level images within one hundred kilometres. One video-frame benchmark reports 65.6 percent within a kilometre for clips from one platform and 6.4 percent for clips from another. The obvious deflation, that benchmark images were seen in training, does not explain the capability: on photographs collected by the authors and not drawn from any public source, frontier models still name the city about 60 percent of the time, and freshly taken photographs of Seoul are located about as well as Street View images of the same city. The author separates five variables that published results leave unfixed (image population, harm radius, adversary configuration, counterfactual baseline, and the unit of exposure), shows that defences are mostly scored against a fixed adversary although a published photograph must resist every later one, and proposes an exposure protocol that states each variable before a number is reported.

title: Coarse-to-Fine Dyadic Sampling: An Exact First-Hit Result and an Exploratory QAOA Benchmark
abstract: This preprint introduces two deterministic coarse-to-fine dyadic sampling strategies and presents an exact first-hit expectation for contiguous target regions, supported by Lean formal verification. Their application to QAOA parameter optimization is explored through reproducible MaxCut simulations and comparisons with classical optimization methods. The results highlight potential applications, limitations, and directions for further research.

title: Non-LLM Continual-Learning AI: From Instrument Readings to a Balloon's Lift
abstract: Tersive White Paper 2. Tersive is a reasoning system that works from a confined body of knowledge and accepts only what it can test. No LLM is used in its reasoning. What it discovered. Tersive was given four instruments with meaningless names and a sealed sample of gas. It was not told what the instruments measured, that a law existed, or that the law fails anywhere. From its own experiments it found the ideal gas law, including its constant. It also found absolute zero by extrapolation, with no limit given: all six runs’ 95% intervals contain −273.15 °C. When the instrument ranges were widened without warning, it refuted its own claim that the law holds everywhere. It then described where the law holds, placing argon’s edge within 0.4 °C of argon’s critical temperature. What it did with it. Tersive kept the law as established knowledge. It then used it, together with standard physics it was given, to predict the lift of a sealed envelope of gas in air, a question it had never seen. Air’s density was never given; Tersive computed it from its own law. Across 630 questions its predictions agreed with CoolProp real-gas references to within 0.29% of the displaced air’s weight. Helium’s lift was within 0.23% in every case, and it predicted that argon sinks. Continual learning. In one investigation Tersive completed a full cycle: it acquired a law by experiment and kept it; it used that law as a premise in a new question; it recognised where its knowledge ran out and reported exactly what was missing; it placed new general facts whose connection to the problem it was not told; it completed the answer, with no change to its reasoning machinery and no loss of earlier abilities. These are internal experiments and have not been peer reviewed. Next steps: replication on data chosen by an outside party, and a test in which a gap in Tersive’s knowledge triggers its own experiments. Continues Tersive White Paper 1 (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24371620).

title: Forecasts that change the future: a closed timelike curve model on quantum hardware
abstract: Published forecasts can bring about the outcomes they announce or provoke responses that avert them. We ask which forecasts remain consistent once people act on them, by conditioning forecasts on agreement with the outcomes they induce. Under a uniform forecast prior, each retained forecast is weighted by its probability of coming true. This rule can be implemented by quantum postselection in a closed timelike curve model built from quantum teleportation. Deutsch's stationary rule gives different weights. In a stylised recession model with a strongly self-defeating response, the recession forecast receives weight 0.0001 under agreement conditioning and 0.30 under the stationary rule. Under a uniform prior the two rules coincide when the outcome ignores the forecast. The rule is classically computable, so the hardware experiment tests how faithfully a processor implements it and gives no computational advantage. Its plan was published before two confirmatory sessions, which ran on IBM Kingston on consecutive days. After readout mitigation the plan's tests of leakage, acceptance and equivalence to a classical filter were met, and a separate witness certified entanglement in the primary circuits. Where the response always averts a forecast recession, the forecast that should be excluded retained weight 0.011 with one two-qubit gate, 0.027 (95% interval 0.015 to 0.039) with two to three and 0.062 with five to seven. Without readout mitigation the second figure is 0.070, above the limit of 0.05. A classically correlated pair in place of the entangled pair gave 0.021.

title: Tsallis Entropy-Regularized Yang-Type Fuzzy c -Directions
abstract: This study proposes Tsallis entropy-regularized Yang-type fuzzy c -directions (TYFCD), which is a fuzzy clustering algorithm designed for spherical data on a unit hypersphere, in which directional information plays a central role. The proposed method is based on the von Mises–Fisher (vMF) distribution and extends the conventional Yang-type fuzzy c -directions (YFCD) by introducing Tsallis entropy regularization into its objective function. This formulation provides additional fuzzification control while retaining YFCD as a special case, thereby generalizing the original framework. The influence of the fuzzification parameters on the fuzzy classification function and the resulting decision boundary was analyzed using a low-dimensional artificial dataset. Extensive experiments on high-dimensional artificial datasets demonstrated that TYFCD exhibits significantly improved robustness compared with existing methods, particularly with low-concentration parameters and severely imbalanced cluster size ratios, where conventional approaches often suffer from numerical instability. Furthermore, experiments on 12 real datasets confirmed that YFCD performs poorly on datasets with extremely high-dimensional settings, whereas TYFCD often achieves higher clustering accuracy than a mixture of vMF distributions and a limiting variant of TYFCD. These results indicate that Tsallis entropy regularization effectively enhances the flexibility and stability of fuzzy clustering for spherical data.

title: CxLSTM: Deploying xLSTM-Based Custom Keyword Spotting to Edge Devices
abstract: Keyword spotting (KWS) serves as the critical entry point for voice interaction in intelligent systems. Traditional KWS systems rely on predefined keywords with limited customization, whereas existing custom keyword spotting (CKWS) approaches incur heavy computational overhead, limiting their deployment on resource-limited edge devices. To address these challenges, we present CxLSTM, an optimized extended LSTM module with only 57.6K parameters, 318.6 KB static memory, 593.1 KB peak memory, and 3.54 MACs per inference. Based on CxLSTM, we propose an on-device CKWS method and perform extensive experiments. In offline evaluation, the proposed method obtains an equal error rate (EER) of 0.27 and an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.78 on the public Google Speech Commands V2 dataset. Superior performance is further validated on a private Mandarin dataset, yielding an EER of 0.06 and an AUC of 0.98. Furthermore, in real-world tests for Mandarin CKWS across three scenarios, the proposed method achieves a recognition accuracy above 95% on Android devices, with a false alarm rate below 0.75/24 h and an average latency of 2.1 ms. When deployed on STM32 microcontrollers, it maintains an accuracy of over 92.3%, with moderately increased false alarms (15.8/24 h) and latency (264.7 ms). Despite performance degradation on low-power microcontrollers due to limited hardware resources, the proposed CKWS method still enables efficient voice interaction on edge devices.

title: Leveraging large language models for cross-cultural innovation research: a cost-effective approach to understanding market perceptions
abstract: Purpose This study assesses how Large Language Models (LLMs) can support cross-cultural market sensing by approximating social survey responses. Design/methodology/approach Responses from five LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, LLaMA, DeepSeek) were compared with the European Social Survey (ESS) Round 11 data for nine questions on gender perceptions in healthcare, employment, and law enforcement in Spain and Finland. Statistical similarity was assessed using the Jensen–Shannon Distance (JSD), Hellinger Distance (HD), and Relative Mean Absolute Difference (RMAD). Findings LLM outputs can approximate survey distributions but cannot substitute for them; in 17 of 18 question–country pairs, at least one model attained high or very high similarity (JSD and HD < 0.2; RMAD <5%). This represents the upper envelope of the five-model portfolio rather than the performance of any single model selected. Models replicated personal experiences better than collective cultural perceptions. No model consistently outperformed across contexts, and substantial divergence across model-question combinations made this instability a central finding. Research limitations/implications This study covers two countries and one thematic module. Future research could examine other contexts and domains. Practical implications LLMs can support lower-cost preliminary market sensing, with validation across multiple models. Social implications LLMs can broaden access to faster, lower-cost cross-cultural research but require human oversight and validation. Originality/value This study provides a systematic multi-model benchmark against probability-sampled cross-national survey data. Its contribution is empirical and methodological, with an exploratory dynamic capability interpretation and an application of generative AI to organisational market sensing.

title: Multilingual Emotion Profiling of Large Language Models Through Literary Texts and Persona Conditioning
abstract: This paper examines whether multilingual prompt-and-text conditions materially alter large language model (LLM) emotion evaluation rather than merely rephrasing the same task. Using OpenRouter as a unified inference layer, we evaluated six contemporary LLMs under three full-language conditions (Japanese, English, and Traditional Chinese), three literary texts, four personas, and three repeated API calls per condition. Each completion rated four emotional dimensions — Interesting, Surprise, Sadness, and Anger — and provided a brief rationale. The design comprised 648 planned evaluations (6 models × 3 languages × 3 texts × 4 personas × 3 trials). The final combined dataset contained 648 valid records, comprising 631 original records and 17 replacement records obtained under a repair amendment registered after the main run and before the patch run. Descriptive summaries and preregistered ordinary least squares analyses with HC3 robust standard errors showed that text content was a major driver of scores, especially for Sadness and Anger. Simultaneously, model-language interactions were significant for all four emotions, indicating that the effect of the language condition varied substantially across models. English yielded the highest mean Interesting, Surprise, and Sadness scores, whereas Japanese yielded the highest mean Anger score. However, these aggregate patterns mask the strong model-specific contrasts. The findings show that multilingual literary evaluation is shaped by both the text itself and the model processing of its translation. This study contributes a multilingual literary emotion benchmark, a preregistered and repair-aware evaluation pipeline, and evidence that multilingual conditions are substantive experimental factors for LLM emotion profiling.

title: Code and clip-level scores: Short-reference voice cloning against speaker verification and anti-spoofing (English–Thai)
abstract: Experiment and analysis code, configuration, fixed thresholds and all non-audio clip-level scores for an offline evaluation of F5-TTS and OpenVoice V2 voice clones against four speaker verifiers and two spoofing countermeasures, using English and Thai recordings from Mozilla Common Voice Scripted Speech 27.0. Includes the window-averaging, silence-trimming and speaker-level sensitivity analyses, and a script (reproduce_tables.py) that recomputes the paper’s main tables. Speakers appear only as pseudonymous run codes; no audio, speaker embeddings, Common Voice file names, contributor identifiers or prompt text are included.

title: AI Policy Research: A New Inquiry
abstract: AI policy is proliferating in universities worldwide, yet AI policy research remains heavily descriptive, cataloguing institutional responses without examining the capacities required to make policy well. This Element argues that the missing capacity is AI policy literacy, the institutional capability to interrogate AI policy as text, discourse, and practice, and to attend to how authority, inequality, and time shape what governance can achieve. Drawing on policy sciences, applied linguistics, and decolonial thought, it develops a six-dimension framework for AI policy literacy. It also demonstrates that AI policies are simultaneously language policies, and that the absence of AI policy research in language education is creating deeper digital divides and knowledge injustices. Treating AI as cognitive infrastructure rather than a tool to be regulated, this Element proposes technodiversity as the orienting principle for governance aligned with universities' educational and social purposes. This title is also available as Open Access on Cambridge Core.

title: Emotional Expression and Purchase Intention in RED Beauty-Related Comments: An Exploratory Comment-Based Analysis
abstract: This study explores how emotional expression and purchase intention are reflected in beauty-related user comments on RED, a major Chinese social media and e-commerce platform. Using 4,371 beauty-related comments, this study applies sentiment analysis, bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT)-based validation, linguistic feature detection, and qualitative coding to examine comment-level consumer expressions. The results show that the overall sentiment was positively inclined but heterogeneous. Sentiment intensity alone did not significantly predict purchase intention. Instead, specific linguistic features, such as emotional adverbs, repeated characters, and information-seeking expressions, played a more important role in indicating consumer interest. In addition, different beauty-related content themes were associated with different response patterns. Comments under “must-buy” posts showed stronger purchase-intention signals, while skincare-related comments showed more information-oriented responses. These findings suggest that purchase intention in RED beauty-related comments is often expressed through subtle linguistic cues rather than strong emotional polarity. This study contributes to social media marketing research by showing the limitations of sentiment-based approaches and the value of comment-level linguistic analysis. The findings also provide practical implications for marketers seeking to identify consumer interest in online communities.

title: Verified schedule switching for crosstalk identification in quantum error correction
abstract: Open-source implementation of verified schedule switching: syndrome-extraction units that share gates and gate order but differ in which operations overlap are verified against a declared set of crosstalk couplings, and switching between them identifies concurrency-induced ZZ couplings from detector statistics, monitors the observation model, and selects the unit used for protection. Includes the Stim-based compiler and noise model, fault-distance verification, the exact parity observation model, identification, finite-sample tests, residual monitoring, a protection-under-drift experiment with PyMatching, all result files and figure scripts.

title: Calibrating the Machine: A Distributional Benchmark of Large Language Model and Human Judgments of Antisemitism
abstract: We ask three questions about large language models (LLMs) and antisemitism. When LLMs make judgments about antisemitism, whose judgments do they most closely resemble, if anyone's at all? Do people's and LLMs' written definitions of antisemitism match how they judge content as antisemitic, and is the discrepancy larger for people or for LLMs? And what is associated with people's antisemitism judgments and with any discrepancy between their definitions and their judgments? We will compare twelve LLMs with a probability-based NORC AmeriSpeak sample of U.S. residents aged 13 and older, including an oversample of Jewish adults, and with a panel of antisemitism experts. The public answered, and the LLMs and experts will answer, the same two questions: a written definition of what makes a statement or belief antisemitic, and antisemitism judgments from 0 (Not antisemitic at all) to 4 (Very antisemitic) of 35 social-media-style posts. The study has 35 research questions. Six are primary and have no directional predictions: whether the LLMs' antisemitism judgments resemble those of the public and those of antisemitism experts, which of the two they are closer to, whether written definitions of antisemitism match their authors' antisemitism judgments for the public and for the LLMs, and whether the discrepancy between definitions and judgments differs between the LLMs and the public. The other 29 questions are secondary.

title: Quote Before You Run: Cost Governance, Reproducibility and Evidence Handling for Agent-Callable Marketing Research Tools
abstract: AI assistants can now call paid research tools on their own through interfaces such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP). For marketing research this creates three practical risks: an agent can spend money faster than its operator expects, stochastic AI-answer data can be read as a single fact, and an empty or failed result can be turned into an invented finding. This technical report proposes ten design requirements for agent-callable paid research tools, compares them with the publicly documented behaviour of one such service (MARqentic), analyses its published credit plans including the marginal price of each plan step, and proposes an evaluation protocol including the number of repeated runs needed to estimate how often an AI engine mentions a brand within a stated margin. No new experiments are reported. Statements about the service come from its public pages as retrieved on 20 November 2026 and were not independently tested. Competing interests: the authors are affiliated with MARqentic (marqentic.com), the service described.

title: Improved TextRank Algorithm Combined with Word2Vec for Extractive Text Summarization and Keyword Extraction
abstract: Aiming at the shortcomings of traditional TextRank algorithm neglecting semantic relationship and context information in extractive text summarization, this paper aims to improve the quality of summaries by combining BERT model with multi-feature fusion. Methodologically, this paper uses BERT to generate sentence vectors to optimize similarity calculation, fuses position features (such as first and last paragraph weight calculation), keyword features (based on TF-IDF and keyword table), clue word features and title features to construct a weight transfer matrix, and enhances keyword extraction with the help of Word2Vec model. At the same time, this paper introduces an improved MMR algorithm to deal with redundancy. The results show that the model reaches 49.3, 24.7, and 46.2 on ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L, respectively, and the redundancy of the model decreases to 0.05. Moreover, the manual evaluation relevance/coherence/conciseness scores of the model all exceed 4.3, the model’s keyword extraction F1 value is the highest 65.2 (for scientific papers), and the model’s multilingual scenario ROUGE-L reaches 44.7 (for German). The conclusion proves that the model significantly improves the statistical accuracy and interpretability of features, and its contribution lies in proposing an efficient and robust extractive framework. However, the model’s ultra-long text processing (such as the completeness rate of key information in the 10,000-word manual) and noisy data adaptability are insufficient. Therefore, it is necessary to optimize the integration of dynamic weight adjustment and generative methods in the future.

title: Sharp Information Limits for Gaussian Covariance Mixtures under Partial Observation
abstract: We determine the small-noise expansion of the maximal relative entropy between a centered Gaussian covariance mixture and the Gaussian law with the same covariance. We prove a formula for the constant term at every positive definite barycenter feasible in a compact semialgebraic covariance set. For a five-cycle of pair observations, we find the optimal rank mixture and characterize saturation under small observation errors. We determine the critical sample scale and optimal limiting power for distinguishing two models with the same full covariance, and analyze uniform smoothing at the singular barycenter.

title: A METHODOLOGICAL FRAMEWORK FOR DEVELOPING AN INFORMATION SECURITY CULTURE IN ENTERPRISES
abstract: This study examines the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in digital games in the contemporary era. The digital gaming industry is continuously evolving under the influence of technological advancements, and AI is one of the most significant drivers of this transformation. In digital games, AI is applied in numerous areas, including improving the behavior of non-player characters (NPCs), dynamically adjusting difficulty levels, generating game content, and personalizing the player experience. The aim of this study is to investigate the areas in which AI is used in digital games and to evaluate its impact on the player experience. A literature review method was employed, and the development and application areas of AI in the digital gaming industry were analyzed. The findings indicate that AI technologies enhance the realism of games, strengthen player interaction, and contribute substantially to replay ability. Furthermore, AI-supported systems were found to increase user satisfaction by offering players more personalized and dynamic experiences. According to the findings, AI technologies play a strategic role in the development of digital games. In the future, AI will remain one of the key factors shaping game design and the player experience. Accordingly, greater investment by game developers in AI-based solutions will enable them to gain a competitive advantage within the industry.

In digital games, AI is applied in numerous areas, including improving the behavior of non-player characters (NPCs), dynamically adjusting difficulty levels, generating game content, and personalizing the player experience. The aim of this study is to investigate the areas in which AI is used in digital games and to evaluate its impact on the player experience. A literature review method was employed, and the development and application areas of AI in the digital gaming industry were analyzed. The findings indicate that AI technologies enhance the realism of games, strengthen player interaction, and contribute substantially to replay ability. Furthermore, AI-supported systems were found to increase user satisfaction by offering players more personalized and dynamic experiences. According to the findings, AI technologies play a strategic role in the development of digital games. In the future, AI will remain one of the key factors shaping game design and the player experience. Accordingly, greater investment by game developers in AI-based solutions will enable them to gain a competitive advantage within the industry.

title: 2026-11-15 The Hardware and Software Architecture of Human Forward Momentum: A Decomposition–Combination Framework for Cognitive and Civilizational Evolution
abstract: AbstractHuman progress is constrained not merely by resource scarcity or technological limits, but by the architecture of information processing—encompassing both the “hardware” of biological cognition and the “software” of conceptual systems. Here we propose a unified framework in which civilizational forward momentum emerges from the coupling between hardware information-processing capacity and software representational flexibility. The hard- ware layer comprises the brain’s neural network and a hypothesized cardiac–blood quantum information-processing system; the software layer comprises conceptual structures that can either rigidify into constraints or become subject to decomposition–combination operations. Drawing on information theory, quantum biology, and historical analysis, we argue that civ- ilizational stagnation occurs when conceptual “justice” structures solidify faster than hard- ware can decompose and recombine them. Conversely, progress arises when the software of thought is decomposed into minimal informational units and recombined at higher organi- zational levels. We present (i) a mathematical model of constraint entropy and decomposi- tion potential, (ii) a computational benchmark comparing classical bit-based and quantum superposition-based information processing, and (iii) testable predictions regarding cardiac quantum coherence, innovation metrics, and artificial-intelligence generalization. Our simu- lations indicate that for high-dimensional semantic recombination tasks, quantum processing reduces operation counts by orders of magnitude relative to classical processing. We conclude that the transition from neural-network to quantum information processing, paired with adecomposition–combination methodology, defines the next frontier of human evolution.

title: Topic Modelling for Biomedical Literature Retrieval via a Dual-Stream Embedding Framework
abstract: The rapid expansion of biomedical literature has created substantial challenges in retrieving and synthesizing relevant knowledge, particularly for novice and interdisciplinary users. Conventional keyword-based methods often lack semantic depth, whereas traditional topic modelling techniques struggle to capture domain-specific contexts and rarely integrate structured metadata, such as medical subject headings (MeSH). To address these limitations, this study introduces a dual-stream embedding framework that integrates unstructured textual content with curated biomedical metadata using transformer-based encoders and a parameterized fusion mechanism. The architecture combines contextual semantics from article titles and abstracts with expert-annotated MeSH descriptors and incorporates a large language model to generate concise and human-readable topic labels. Experimental results show that three of the four evaluated embedding configurations outperformed the single-stream baseline and that the dual-stream fusion surpassed all ablation models built from the same inputs. The best configuration, Dual PubMedBERT, achieved the highest overall topic modelling quality, improving the combined measure of topic coherence and topic diversity by 7.3% relative to the baseline. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of integrating contextual textual embeddings with structured biomedical metadata using the proposed fusion mechanism. This approach is scalable, reproducible, and domain-adaptable, providing both a methodological advancement in semantic topic modelling and a practical foundation for the development of biomedical information retrieval systems, semantic search engines, and thematic exploration tools across knowledge-intensive domains.

title: Posterior Matching Distillation
abstract: Diffusion distillation accelerates image and video generation by compressing a pretrained teacher's iterative sampling process into a few network evaluations. Distribution-based methods achieve this by matching the student's output distribution to the teacher's. This matching is often driven by reverse-KL objectives, whose mode-seeking bias favors dominant teacher modes at the expense of diversity across samples. We introduce Posterior Matching Distillation (PMD), a new member of the distribution-based distillation family that combines mode-covering posterior sampling with any-step generation. At zero population loss, PMD recovers the teacher's full posterior of clean images at each trained noise level. Its stochastic student supports any-step sampling budgets within the trained timestep grid without further training. To learn these posteriors, PMD matches exponentially reweighted averages of student samples conditioned on a fixed noisy state to corresponding teacher posterior means. Under Gaussian corruption, exponentially tilted posterior mean is a single teacher evaluation at a shifted input. We prove that, matching tilted means over an open neighborhood uniquely identifies the full posterior. PMD thus supervises the entire conditional distribution through a family of mean constraints, without any auxiliary student-score network. Experiments on SDXL and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B demonstrate that PMD achieves the best FID among 4-step methods on both models, while maintaining competitive or leading performance across prompt-alignment and perceptual-quality metrics.

title: RL Post-Training in Diffusion Transformers Is Activation Steering
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training substantially improves the visual quality, text rendering, and compositional accuracy of diffusion transformers. Because capabilities such as rendering requested text or composing multiple objects are inherently prompt-dependent, a natural hypothesis is that improving them requires learning complex, input-dependent transformations. To isolate how much of these gains an input-independent shift explains, we probe each RL-tuned model with a deliberately simple parameterization: a fixed set of steering vectors added to the block outputs of the frozen base model. On SD3.5-M, these vectors hold 65x fewer parameters than the RL-tuned LoRA (0.29M against 18.8M). We fit them to match the velocity predictions of public RL-tuned checkpoints, with no reward in the objective. Although the vectors are identical for every prompt, token, and sampling seed, they recover 90.0-96.3% of the reward gains of six RL-tuned image models, and 89.8% and 111.9% on two RL-tuned video models. Initialized at zero and trained with online RL, the vectors alone exceed the reward gains of weight-based RL on text rendering (OCR) and human preference (PickScore) on SD3.5-M. A constant shift thus suffices for most of the gain of policy-gradient RL post-training: without new input-dependent transformations, it steers the pretrained generator toward what it can already compute.

title: PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience
abstract: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experience to revise them for mastery. Starting from an initial game, PlayCraft alternates between playing and crafting. In the playing stage, a player agent watches the game screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes while retaining memory. After each episode, it reports its progress, outcomes, decisions, and reflections. In the crafting stage, a crafter agent uses these reports to revise the game. It estimates player abilities, predicts performance at different proficiency levels, and compares those predictions with a target learning progression. It diagnoses the game and addresses the gaps by giving players meaningful opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. We evaluate games in fresh runs with player agents across three intelligence settings, measuring learning gain and learning slope. Compared with the initial games, PlayCraft yields larger learning gains and steeper learning slopes in most games. It also outperforms the baselines on the macro-average of each metric at every intelligence setting.

title: One Prior, Two Dynamics: Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning
abstract: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and forward dynamics. We introduce O$^{2}$LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck, O$^{2}$LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O$^{2}$LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance. Our findings suggest a broader paradigm for latent-action learning: repurposing pretrained video models to discover transferable actions and predict their consequences.

title: AgentRoboCritic: Understanding the Capability of Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control
abstract: Frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated strong capabilities in controlling robots directly via low-level numerical actions without high-level primitives. However, existing benchmarks report only episode-level success rates, which show neither how these agents succeed nor where they fail. In this paper, we present a systematic action-level analysis of frontier agents on direct robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks. We introduce AgentRoboCritic, an intent-grounded critique framework in which the policy agent states a local intent alongside each action, and a critic evaluates the action's outcome and failure mode against this intent. Our action-level analysis demonstrates the promising capabilities of frontier agents on direct robot control, including closed-loop recovery from local execution failures, reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. It also identifies their current limitations, including task-relevant physical execution bottlenecks such as grasping and alignment, and uneven recovery across failure modes. Finally, we validate our critic on a 400-action human-annotated benchmark and release a dataset of 12,844 annotated actions alongside a fine-tuned open-source critic, Muse-Glimmer-30B, whose failure-mode accuracy rises from 32.58% to 74.24%, enabling low-cost action-level analysis.

title: Depth Pro 2: Sharp and Temporally Consistent Metric Monocular Depth
abstract: We present Depth Pro 2, an approach to estimating dense metric depth for images and video at full resolution. By analyzing prior methods for monocular depth estimation, we find that they commonly trade off temporal consistency and boundary sharpness: multi-frame methods favor consistency, single-frame methods favor sharpness. To overcome this trade-off, we train a single, scalable network that processes both images and video and predicts depth maps at native resolution. Depth Pro 2 produces depth maps that are metrically accurate, sharp, and temporally consistent all at once, outperforming prior work in all of these dimensions. We release a family of models that define a new Pareto frontier in terms of metric accuracy, sharpness, temporal consistency, and runtime. We release code and weights at https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-depth-pro-2/

title: Coda-DaVinci: Reimagining Video Generation with Code2Video
abstract: Code2Video uses agent-authored 3D proxies to guide video generation, enabling explicit control over structure and dynamics. However, how to construct proxies and prompts for optimal downstream quality remains underexplored, as do the capabilities and limitations of this paradigm. Through controlled experiments and blinded human evaluation, we study proxy granularity, physics simulation, and prompting. The results reveal task-dependent trade-offs: coarse proxies favor natural motion, while medium-grained proxies favor consistency. Physics simulation and proxy-aligned prompting further improve average quality. Guided by these findings, we introduce Coda-DaVinci, a task-adaptive agentic framework for Code2Video generation that selects between proxy-guided and direct generation, adapts modeling granularity to each entity, and coordinates simulation with proxy-grounded prompting. Its multi-agent harness preserves scene assets and guides repairs through visual inspection and independent review. Experiments demonstrate leading instruction following on VTR and scene consistency on R2M, improved physical plausibility over direct generation, and higher visual realism than the compared Code2Video baselines. Long-video evaluations further show gains in event structure and consistency across successive interactions, while revealing limitations in transition stability and adherence to scene settings.

The results reveal task-dependent trade-offs: coarse proxies favor natural motion, while medium-grained proxies favor consistency. Physics simulation and proxy-aligned prompting further improve average quality. Guided by these findings, we introduce Coda-DaVinci, a task-adaptive agentic framework for Code2Video generation that selects between proxy-guided and direct generation, adapts modeling granularity to each entity, and coordinates simulation with proxy-grounded prompting. Its multi-agent harness preserves scene assets and guides repairs through visual inspection and independent review. Experiments demonstrate leading instruction following on VTR and scene consistency on R2M, improved physical plausibility over direct generation, and higher visual realism than the compared Code2Video baselines. Long-video evaluations further show gains in event structure and consistency across successive interactions, while revealing limitations in transition stability and adherence to scene settings.

title: Probing the "Conscious" Mind: Selective Access and Global Workspace in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual and textual information, but their outputs do not reveal internal concept representations. Global workspace theory (GWT) proposes that information is selected from parallel brain processes, integrated in a shared workspace, and made available to specialised processes. We introduce the Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens), a multimodal Jacobian lens, to study these functions in VLM concept processing. Its vision encoder and language decoder lenses map intermediate states to a shared semantic space defined by the decoder's output vocabulary to compare concept accessibility across modalities. MC-Lens supports internal concept interventions to examine the role of accessed concepts in downstream computation. (i) Accessibility and selective access. Multimodal concept information is readable in intermediate states and selectively accessible as tasks require. We extend "readout carriers" from one name token to a token set to better capture and express concept information and support counterfactual experiments. (ii) Concepts in downstream computation. Counterfactual experiments show that accessed concept information participates in downstream computation and reasoning. (iii) Development of cross-modal alignment and selective access. We develop two J-space metrics tracking the development of cross-modal concept alignment more clearly than hidden state cosine in controlled VLM training. The experiment also shows that reliable selective access develops later than concept accessibility. (iv) Shared functions across models. Across VLM families and sizes, we find shared patterns of concept accessibility, query-dependent selectivity and cross-task intervention effects despite differences in internal organisation. These findings offer an experimental basis to study GWT in multimodal artificial systems and how it can guide cross-modal alignment improvements.

title: AURA: AUdio-dRiven streaming Avatar
abstract: Current audio-driven video diffusion models can synthesize realistic talking-head videos but generally require dozens of diffusion denoising steps over multi-second video chunks, making them unsuitable for streaming applications such as voice assistants and virtual avatars, where low-latency and online causal generation are required properties. AURA generates video chunk by chunk with a rolling KV cache, requiring only the audio of the current chunk to start generating, rather than a multi-second audio look-ahead like bidirectional models. It comes in two sizes: AURA 1.3B streams 576p video in real time on a single GPU (20.7 fps for a 16 Hz playback rate), making it suited to interactive avatar applications, and AURA 5B streams 720p video at 9.7 fps. Our two-stage distillation pipeline first aligns the causal student with the teacher, by training it to match the teacher's trajectories with fewer diffusion steps and a chunk-wise sliding window causal attention mask, then applies Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) with backward simulation to close the remaining quality gap. On standard talking-head benchmarks, AURA 1.3B runs 23x faster than its own bidirectional teacher and reaches a quality comparable to TalkVerse at a lower resolution, and AURA 5B matches its TalkVerse teacher at 720p while running 17x faster. To support reproducibility and further research on streaming avatar generation, we release the weights of both models along with a dataset of 30K synthetic videos and their precomputed teacher trajectories.

title: Direct3D-V3: Latent-Free Diffusion Transformers in the Native Voxel Domain
abstract: Native 3D generation has largely been built around latent diffusion, with recent advances concentrating on stronger variational autoencoders (VAE) and increasingly elaborate latent representations, from vecset and triplanes to structured sparse voxels. Despite their architectural differences, these methods all share the same premise: geometry is first compressed into a latent space and only then modeled by the generator. We take a different route and propose Direct3D-V3, a latent-free diffusion transformer (DiT) framework that discards the VAE altogether and operates in the native voxel domain, directly modeling raw SDF voxel grids during both training and sampling. To make this direct voxel formulation geometrically reliable, we introduce an implicit manifold regularization over neighboring voxels to suppress non-watertight surfaces, and convert predicted SDF grids into meshes via Marching Cubes so that rendered normal losses can supervise the model directly from its predicted SDF. To improve alignment between the conditioning image and generated geometry, Direct3D-V3 also predicts the camera parameters of the conditioning image as an auxiliary task, encouraging the DiT to learn the mapping from image observations to 3D shape. This latent-free design removes the reconstruction bottleneck, brings training under an objective in the native voxel domain, and yields meshes with substantially richer local detail. The predicted camera and native SDF voxel output further make Direct3D-V3 extensible to generative reconstruction, where diffusion is interleaved with normal-guided refinement to improve alignment with the observed view while the generative prior completes unseen regions. Project page: https://dreamtechai.github.io/Direct3D-V3.

title: AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model a Better Teacher
abstract: Task success alone does not specify which behaviors post-training should reinforce. Even successful teacher trajectories can contain unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, or superficial verification. We propose Skill-FT (Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning), which uses natural-language skills to suppress undesirable habits and elicit underrepresented effective behaviors during teacher rollouts, then fine-tunes a target model on the resulting trajectories. We introduce AutoMaster, an autonomous post-training system in which an LLM agent develops these interventions through trajectory analysis, skill design, data selection, and feedback from rollouts and target-model evaluation. Across Terminal, Search, and software engineering tasks with 4B and 9B target models, AutoMaster improves mean performance over Vanilla SFT on successful unguided teacher trajectories by 1.42-8.99 percentage points, with the teacher, task pool, training set size, and SFT recipe held fixed. Together with the ablations and trajectory analyses, these results suggest that behavioral shaping can make a fixed model a more effective teacher. We further find that retaining skill instructions during SFT yields higher mean performance than removing them across all six settings, despite their absence at evaluation and identical supervised outputs. These findings suggest that preserving skill context as part of a training demonstration can support better behavioral internalization.

title: GLiDE: A Fast, Calibrated Decision Model Distilled from Reasoning Teachers
abstract: Decision models enable fast, confidence-aware decisions by scoring candidate answers in a single forward pass, without generating text or intermediate reasoning. Yet reasoning can substantially improve decision quality, raising the question of whether its benefits can be retained without the cost of generating it. We investigate this question with \textbf{GLiDE}, a family of decision models spanning 0.4B to 27B parameters. Building on Qwen hybrid language models, GLiDE enables bidirectional interactions between the context, question, and candidate answers by removing causal masking from full-attention layers. To transfer reasoning capabilities into single-pass inference, we combine soft-target distillation from multiple teachers, including a reasoning model, with progressive post-training on diverse decision tasks. We further explore parameter-free recurrent depth to increase inference-time computation without generating tokens. Across five model sizes, GLiDE lies on the performance--parameter Pareto frontier of the Hugging Face \DI{}, with each model outperforming evaluated alternatives of equal or smaller size. \dmtwo{} (27B) achieves a hidden-set score of 71.52, with an expected calibration error of 2.0\% and a median latency of 92.9\,ms on a single GPU. Further checkpoint averaging and parameter-free recurrent depth yield GLiDE~27B, which reaches 73.37 with an expected calibration error of 2.1\%.

title: A CPU Inside an LLM: Zero-Gradient Compilation of Exact Circuits into Pretrained Weights
abstract: Pretrained language models (LMs) remain unreliable on exact multi-digit arithmetic without gradient fine-tuning or external tool interpreters. We introduce closed-form, zero-gradient circuit-grafting primitives that compile deterministic computation directly into pretrained LM weights using zero training examples and zero runtime hooks, while bounding per-layer normalization drift and preserving natural-language (NL) competence. Our construction combines three analytical mechanisms: (1) two-layer Mellin-GLU quadrature over bias-free SwiGLU/GeGLU layers, turning unknown per-token RMSNorm scaling into translation along a log-spaced gate grid ($>250\times$ dynamic range) with IEEE 754 error bounds; (2) cross-token scale cancellation via signed Chebyshev Indefinite-RoPE self-sink attention and memoryless SiLU-antisymmetric GatedDeltaNet shifts; and (3) axis-aligned width extension ($d \to d+K$) with $\sqrt{d/(d+K)}$ norm compensation, Base-1000 canonical BPE emission, and differential $(+254,-256)$ tied unembeddings. An automated 5-stage compiler synthesizes 4-8 digit signed $\{+,-,\times\}$ circuits in constant $\mathsf{TC}^0$ depth alongside 3-literal Boolean (100%, $N=1{,}728$; plus 42-layer Gemma 4 E4B audits) and 5-bit Majority/Parity (100%) circuits. On 6-digit arithmetic ($N=1{,}200$, BF16), IBM Granite 4.2 3B (1.07M-1.33M active non-zeros, $\le 0.036\%$) and Alibaba Qwen 3.5 4B (2.25M-2.39M non-zeros, $\le 0.057\%$) reach 99.17% and 100.00% ALU-prefix accuracy (100% with an FP32 sidecar) and 98%-100% mid-sentence resumption, outperforming 12.8K-sample LoRA (42.2% / 61.7%, 0% inline continuation). A factorized block-sparse sidecar holds A100 memory at 7.89 / 10.65 GiB (4.60 / 8.14 GiB under INT8/INT4 + FP32 sidecar) while passing all 14/14 pre-registered $>2$K-token Tango splits ($N=4{,}392$; 0/11,134 OOD triggers).
